summary.text: Sampling bias happens when a sample is collected so that some members of the intended population are more or less likely to be picked than others.
If it is not accounted for, results can wrongly be credited to the thing being studied rather than to the way the sample was gathered.
Typical forms include surveys that leave out whole groups, polls where people choose themselves, and studies that look only at survivors.

facts.label: Core idea
facts.value: Some members have a lower or higher chance of being selected

facts.label: Medical name
facts.value: Medical sources sometimes call it ascertainment bias

facts.label: Self-selection
facts.value: Online and phone-in polls are biased because respondents choose themselves

facts.label: Zero chance
facts.value: Excluding a group entirely gives its members zero probability of selection

items.prompt: A survey of teenage drug use is handed out only in high school classrooms. Why does it give a biased picture of all teenagers?

options.label: Students always lie about drug use on surveys
Teens not enrolled in school never had a chance to be asked
Schools hold too many students to count properly
Teenagers change their habits once a survey arrives

items.explain: Home-schooled students and dropouts are left out, so some members of the population had no chance of being selected.

items.prompt: A reporter interviews people who walk past a downtown corner at noon about their health. Whose voices are likely overrepresented?

options.label: People with chronic illness, who need the most attention
An even mix, since passers-by are effectively random
Only people who live on that exact block
Healthy people, who are more likely to be out of the house

items.explain: People who walk by are more likely to be healthy than those with a chronic illness, so the sample leans toward the healthy.

items.prompt: A website invites visitors to vote in a poll on a hot political issue. Who is most likely to take part?

options.label: People with strong opinions, whose views then get extra weight
A fair cross-section, since anyone could click a button
Mostly people who feel indifferent about the issue
Only visitors the website picked at random

items.explain: Respondents choose themselves, and highly motivated people with strong opinions are overrepresented, which can give extreme views a disproportionate weight.

items.prompt: Someone judges how healthy the economy is by looking only at the companies that exist today. What is missing from that picture?

options.label: Companies that are about to be founded
The very largest firms, which are always excluded
The businesses that failed and no longer exist
The customers of the companies that survive

items.explain: Looking only at survivors ignores subjects that fell out of view, such as failed businesses.

items.prompt: A study of manual laborers' health is used to describe everyone's health. Why will it likely make people look healthier than they are?

options.label: Laborers report their own health less honestly than others
People in poor health are unlikely to hold manual labor jobs
Manual laborers are always older than the general population
Studies of workers include too few participants to judge

items.explain: The study population is likely healthier than the general population, because someone in poor health is unlikely to work as a manual laborer.

items.prompt: In a hospital's records, patients without diabetes more often have some other disease. Why can this pattern be misleading about people in general?

options.label: Every patient had some reason to be admitted, which creates the pattern
Diabetes protects people against most other diseases
Hospitals only record diseases that are rare
Hospital patients are healthier than the general population

items.explain: A hospital sample is less healthy than the general population, and a patient without diabetes must have had some other reason to be there, giving a spurious negative link between diseases.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Sampling bias is a flaw in the way a sample is gathered. Some members of the population a study means to describe end up with a better or worse chance of being picked than others. The sample that results is called biased, because not every individual was equally likely to land in it.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: The danger is a wrong conclusion. If nobody corrects for the bias, a result can be credited to the thing under study when it really comes from how the sample was drawn. One view, not shared by everyone, says sampling bias harms external validity: how well the findings carry over to the whole population.

paragraphs.heading: Other names
paragraphs.text: In medicine the same problem is sometimes called ascertainment bias. Sampling bias is usually counted as one kind of selection bias, though some people keep the two apart. In practice the two names are often swapped freely.

paragraphs.heading: Leaving groups out
paragraphs.text: One form comes from drawing the sample in one particular place. A survey of teenage drug use handed out in high schools misses teens who are home-schooled or have dropped out. A street interview that stops passers-by catches too many healthy people and too few with a chronic illness, who are less often out of the house. When a group is shut out entirely, its members have zero chance of selection, which may be an extreme form of the problem.

paragraphs.heading: Choosing yourself
paragraphs.text: Self-selection bias can arise whenever the people being studied decide for themselves whether to take part. That choice may be tied to traits that affect the study, so those who join are not typical. People with strong opinions or deep knowledge are keener to spend time on a survey. So online and phone-in polls overrepresent the highly motivated, hear less from the indifferent, and give extreme views too much weight. For this reason such polls are regarded as unscientific.

paragraphs.heading: Survivors and hospitals
paragraphs.text: Survivorship bias looks only at what survived and ignores what dropped out of view. Judging the economy by the firms that exist today, for instance, leaves out every business that failed. Berkson's fallacy is the hospital version: a study population drawn from patients is less healthy than people in general. This can produce a false negative link between diseases, since a patient without diabetes is more likely to have some other illness, such as cholecystitis, that brought them in.
